blocks.title: When the bars feel busy
blocks.content:
A road rider reaches the first rough patch of a gravel ride. The front end moves more than it does on pavement, so the rider straightens the elbows and pushes down on the hoods. Steering gets harder as each bump moves the rider’s shoulders.

Start with an easier patch and a slower pace. Keep a secure hold on the bars, but give your elbows room to move.

A death grip is an understandable reaction to an unfamiliar surface. It can also leave your arms too stiff to make small steering adjustments. You need control of the bars and access to the brakes, with enough movement in your elbows to respond to the ground.

Notice where your weight goes. Your saddle carries much of it while you are seated; your feet share the load. If you press hard into the hoods, ease the pace and reset your position. The goal is a secure grip without using the bars as a brace.

blocks.label: Support through your feet, secure hands
blocks.content: On smooth, flat gravel at an easy pace, keep both hands wrapped around the hoods. Notice the contact under your feet. Bend your elbows slightly, breathe normally, and check that you can steer and brake without a sudden shift in weight. Do not open your hands or release the bars as a test.

blocks.title: Set a position you can steer from
blocks.description: Use these cues on easy ground before trying a rough section.

steps.detail: Pick a clear, quiet stretch where you can slow or stop without pressure from traffic.
Wrap your hands around the hoods or drops and keep the brake levers within reach.
Let your saddle and feet support you rather than leaning hard on your hands.
Keep a small bend in the arms. If the front end feels unpredictable, slow down or use smoother ground.

blocks.content: During a race, the rider ahead rolls over washboard faster than you want to. Leave space, look for a smoother visible line, and choose your own pace. A secure grip and movable arms matter more than copying their speed.

blocks.title: Feet and hands check
blocks.description: Compare your contact with the pedals, saddle, and bars at an easy pace. Keep a secure grip throughout.

variants.label: Flat, open practice area
steps: Choose a flat, familiar route with room to stop.
Ride easily with both hands wrapped around the hoods. Notice whether you are pressing down on the bars.
Let your elbows bend slightly and keep your feet engaged on the pedals. Do not lift your fingers from the controls.
Stop safely and note what made steering feel easier. If your hands hurt or go numb, check your position and bike fit before repeating.

proof_gate.description: You can maintain a secure grip and reach the brakes without bracing on the bars.
proof_gate.target: Repeat on a familiar, low-traffic surface at a comfortable pace.

blocks.title: Relaxed grip, secure hands
blocks.description: Practice removing excess tension while keeping control of the bike.

variants.label: Flat, open practice area
steps: Ride slowly with both hands securely on the bars.
Notice your grip. Ease excess tension without opening your hands or moving fingers away from the controls.
Make a wide, slow turn and a gentle stop. Repeat only while steering and braking feel predictable.

proof_gate.description: You can turn and stop smoothly with secure hands and movable elbows.
proof_gate.target: Stop the drill if steering or braking becomes uncertain.

blocks.content:
### If it still feels tense

Do not try to force your shoulders to relax while the bike is moving faster than you can manage. Reduce speed first. Check your line, keep both hands on the bars, and give your elbows room to bend. If hand pain or numbness keeps returning, a fit issue may be part of the problem.

blocks.title: How to Fix Your Body Position on the Gravel Bike
blocks.caption: CX champion demoing gravel body position — watch the neutral, hinged, heavy-feet stance.

blocks.question: Small bumps make you push down on the hoods. What is the useful first adjustment?

options.text: Open your hands to prove the bike can steer itself
Slow down, keep a secure grip, and let your elbows move
Lock your arms and ride faster through the bumps
Look only at the front wheel

blocks.explanation: Choose an easy pace, keep both hands at the controls, and give your arms room to respond.

blocks.content: On your next easy gravel ride, notice when you begin leaning into the hoods. Slow down, reset, and write down whether steering changed.
The next lesson covers rider position. You will use the same secure hands and movable elbows while letting your legs respond to small changes in the ground.
